blindComparison: Shown unlabelled beside a golden-hour Ghost of Tsushima vista — and I am comparing from memory, not against any fetched reference frame; no side-by-side against real reference footage was performed — a stranger picks the reference, and for `wide` and `valley` they do not hesitate. The single reason they give: in ours the distance is a flat colour, in theirs the distance is a surface. Our 1.8 km mountain flank measures a standard deviation of 1.31 luma and a Laplacian of 1.14 over an 8,400-pixel patch (wide, x2180-2320 y430-490) while the flagstone three metres from the camera measures 9.45 — the far range carries one eighth of the near range's texture, so the mountain reads as a paper cutout laid behind the shrine, and the eye resolves the whole vista as a painted backdrop the moment it is asked to travel into it. The reference's distant ridges hold rock, scree, snow-shadow and vegetation banding all the way to the horizon, and that is what makes its scale believable. Our close framings — `torii` and `sun` — are a genuinely different story: the contre-jour in `sun`, the vermilion against the cool plaza, and the lantern spill are competitive work, and a stranger would have to look twice. The verdict is decided by the two framings that have to sell the world, plus one artefact (the stair-stepped black wedge in `hero`) that is visible at thumbnail size on the contact sheet.

findings.problem: The large ground shadow that crosses the plaza in the lower-left third of `hero` has a hard, unfiltered staircase for an edge and a colourless black hole for an interior. Two separate measurements. (1) Edge quantisation: tracking the first pixel below luma 6 along each scanline from x=850 rightward, the boundary holds one identical x value for 5-15 consecutive rows and then jumps 8-22 columns in a single row. Rows y752-848 give the run sequence x997 for 2 rows, x982 for 8, x974 for 7, x967 for 7, x952 for 7, x944 for 5, x922 for 15, x907 for 7, x892 for 7, x884 for 7, x869 for 7, x854 for 7. That is a visible flight of stairs, not a shadow edge, and it survives to thumbnail scale in shots/sheet-phone-r17.png. (2) No ambient in the umbra: box (770,880,40x30) inside reads mean RGB 9.6/8.6/9.5, luma 8.9, minimum 0, R-B of +0.1 — perfectly neutral; box (880,880,40x30) twenty pixels to its right reads 59.8/49.8/47.8, luma 51.8, R-B +12.0. The transition at y=900 runs 58 -> 15 -> 1.8 luma across eight pixels with no penumbra. 10.0% of the region x620-1160 y700-1140 sits below luma 6, and 2.33% of the whole frame is below luma 4. I am NOT filing the disproved claim that shadows are missing or that a shadow with no visible caster is wrong — HANDOFF.md settles both, and at a 13 degree sun a detached shadow 4.33x the caster's height downsun is the correct output. The defect here is the edge filtering and the absence of any sky fill inside the umbra.
findings.why: A shipped title never shows a stepped shadow boundary; the staircase alone reads as a broken build. Worse, a golden-hour shadow that goes to neutral RGB(9,9,10) with zero blue means the shadow side of the frame carries no colour at all, which is the exact opposite of the warm-key/cool-shadow separation E11-VISUALS lists as a principle. In the reference, the shaded flagstone stays blue and you can still read the stone through it; here it is a hole cut in the image.
findings.fix: Two verifiable targets on this same region. (a) Edge: re-measure the boundary run lengths with the same scan (first pixel below luma 6 per row, x from 850 rightward, rows y752-848). No single x value may repeat for more than 2 consecutive rows, and no row-to-row jump may exceed 3 columns. (b) Umbra fill: box (770,880,40x30) must come up to at least luma 18 with B-R of at least +4 (a cool sky-fill tint), while box (880,880,40x30) stays within 5 luma of its current 51.8 so the contrast ratio is not simply flattened. Report both boxes before and after; byte-identical numbers mean the branch you edited does not draw these pixels.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN, do not act on this before disproving it: the step period is roughly 7 rows by 15 columns in a 2532x1170 PNG that was upscaled 1.876x from a 1350x624 render buffer, i.e. roughly 4 by 8 render pixels, which is the scale of a single shadow-map texel projected onto near-camera ground rather than of a filter kernel. If that is right the cause is receiver-side texel footprint on this cascade, not the cascade coverage question that rounds 7, 8 and 15 already killed. Disprove it by measuring the projected texel size at this ground point before changing anything, and report the disproof if it fails.

findings.problem: The distant mountain range, which occupies roughly the top 40% of the `wide` framing and is the entire reason that framing exists, is rendered as an untextured flat fill. Box (2180,430,140x60) on the mountain flank measures mean RGB 197.0/154.0/117.1, luma 160.52, standard deviation 1.31, full range 154.4-170.5 over 8,400 pixels; a mean-absolute-Laplacian over the same box is 1.14. For comparison in the same frame: near ground x400-1200 y1000-1120 is 7.44, and in `hero` the near flagstone x300-900 y1070-1160 is 9.45 and the mid flagstone x1900-2400 y900-960 is 8.10. The far range therefore carries 6.5-8.3x less local detail than every other surface in the review set. A native crop of x2280-2520 y340-520 shows the result plainly: a solid salmon shape with a hard vector-like ridgeline and literally no interior modulation — no rock, no scree, no snow, no vegetation banding, no shading break. This is a different finding from round 16's R16 major, which was that the distant terrain was desaturated; that has moved (this patch now measures saturation 0.405, warm bias R-B +79.9). The colour is fixed and the surface is still missing.
findings.why: E11-VISUALS states the principle without qualification: grain at every scale, no untextured flat surface anywhere in frame. A flat fill at that screen size collapses the vista into a matte painting, and it is the single clearest thing a stranger would name in a blind pick against a Ghost of Tsushima ridgeline. E05-WORLD BM-WORLD-01 also depends on the background plane being a surface rather than a silhouette.
findings.fix: Raise the mean-absolute-Laplacian of box (2180,430,140x60) in `wide` from 1.14 to at least 4.0 and the standard deviation from 1.31 to at least 6, without moving the box mean luma more than 8 from 160.5 and without lifting saturation above 0.45 (the aerial-perspective budget must survive). Verify with the same box and the same Laplacian, and also report the near-ground control box (400,1000,800x120), currently 7.44, to prove the whole frame was not simply sharpened. Round 8 already established that this part of `wide` is macro heightfield at 1000-1080 m, not the 5000 m parallax ridge band, so this is Terrain's surface, not the ridge cylinder.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN: the flatness is scale-selective rather than total — the ridgeline silhouette itself has real second-order structure (round 8 measured 2nd-difference RMS 0.97 px over the same span), so something is producing correct macro geometry with no detail octaves surviving on top of it at this distance. Prove or disprove which octaves reach this range before touching the splat.

findings.problem: The ground cover across the whole playable area reads as bare dirt, not as vegetation, in both open framings. In `wide` a native crop of x1300-2200 y800-1160 shows one continuous low-frequency brown-and-blue smear with a scatter of tiny near-identical dark stubs on it; those stubs are only 2.0% of the sampled area (3,289 of 162,000 pixels below luma 18 in x1300-2200 y820-1000) and mean RGB 12.4/15.7/19.8 against lit ground at 76.0/60.4/53.7 — a cool near-black speck four times darker than the surface it sits on, at one size, in one shape, repeated. Nothing in that half of the frame reads as a plant. In `valley` the problem is the named subject of the shot: what ARCHITECTURE 5 calls a bamboo sea is roughly twenty isolated bare culms, each a dark pole with a leaf tuft only at its extreme tip and nothing at all below it, standing on an unbroken bare plain. Ground block means down the valley floor (10 columns x 4 rows from y470 to y825) run 50 73 96 148 130 108 76 66 59 46 / 58 72 93 119 59 61 45 36 32 21 / 56 70 88 67 36 53 47 40 36 21 / 54 60 76 13 53 67 54 56 37 19 — a smooth exposure gradient with no vegetation mass anywhere in it.
findings.why: Ghost of Tsushima's fields are the most reproduced image in that title and they are a wind-driven volume of grass that the player is inside. Ours is a floor with litter on it. E05-WORLD BM-WORLD-01 needs three separable depth planes per framing and in `valley` the mid-ground plane is simply absent — you can see continuous bare ground from three metres to the treeline with nothing occluding anything, so the shot has a foreground and a background and nothing between. A stranger reads it as an unfinished level, not as a place.
findings.fix: Two targets, both re-measurable from the same boxes. (a) `wide`: in x1300-2200 y820-1000 the fraction of pixels belonging to vegetation must rise from 2.0% to at least 12%, and the mean RGB of those pixels must reach at least luma 30 with a green lead (G-R of at least +6) so they read as plants rather than as dark specks; report the lit-ground control (currently 76.0/60.4/53.7) unchanged within 5 luma. (b) `valley`: the culms must carry foliage below the tip — measure the fraction of pixels inside the culm bounding columns (native x1250-1900, y0-450) that are leaf-coloured, and take it from its current near-zero to at least 25%; and the ground band y470-830 must gain occluding mid-ground mass so that at least 3 of the 10 column blocks in each of the four rows differ from their neighbour by more than 20 luma. Do not solve this by raising fog.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN: the stub population being one size and one shape suggests a single card archetype at a single scale rather than a density shortfall, in which case raising instance count alone will make the litter denser without making it read as vegetation. Test by measuring the size distribution of the connected dark components before deciding whether the fix is count, archetype variety, or card height.

findings.problem: The sun disc renders as a neutral near-white ball on a strongly warm sky, in both framings that contain it, and it is the least saturated object in either frame. `sun`, box (1520,525,40x40) on the disc core: mean RGB 253.3/253.1/244.0, saturation 0.037, R-B +9.4; box (1300,525,40x40) on sky 220 px to its left: 238.5/221.0/156.4, saturation 0.344, R-B +82.1. `valley`, box (930,30,30x30) on the disc: 246.1/246.4/244.7, saturation 0.007, standard deviation 0.58 — a flat neutral plate; box (790,30,30x30) on nearby sky: 223.8/214.7/170.3, saturation 0.239, R-B +53.5. The telemetry in shots/report-r17.json gives the sun colour as [1, 0.412, 0.134], so the source is strongly orange and the pixel is white. This is unchanged from round 16, which measured 0.036 on the same feature and filed it as a minor against src/render/Sky.js; round 16's own disproof then established that Sky.js delivers the disc at saturation 0.238 and that the loss happens downstream in the tone map, and that the only fix is a hue-preserving highlight rolloff which nobody currently owns. It is refiled here as a major because it is the focal point of one of the five framings and it is now the second round it has survived.
findings.why: At a 13 degree elevation the sun is the warmest object in the sky by a wide margin, and every golden-hour reference frame reads it as amber. A white disc on an amber sky is the signature of a clipped tone map, and it drags the whole grade with it — the frame stops reading as sunset light and starts reading as an overexposed photograph. E11-VISUALS asks for a filmic grade, not a glow filter, and this is the one place the grade is visibly failing.
findings.fix: A hue-preserving highlight rolloff on the composited frame, verified on both discs: box (1520,525,40x40) in `sun` must reach saturation of at least 0.20 with R-B of at least +45 while its luma stays above 235, and box (930,30,30x30) in `valley` must reach at least 0.15 saturation from its current 0.007. Report the two sky control boxes (1300,525,40x40) in `sun` and (790,30,30x30) in `valley` unchanged within 0.03 saturation, so the fix is proven to be a highlight rolloff and not a global saturation push. Note the routing is my judgement, not a proof: round 16 showed the disc leaves Sky.js at 0.238 and that the ACES fit returns 255/255/255 at 293 scene-linear, which puts the loss in the grade — if PostFX proves the clip happens before it receives tScene, say so and hand it back with the measurement.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN, and round 16 already partly killed the obvious version: cutting the sky-side peak by 53x returns saturation 0.010, not 0.25, so the disc cannot be rescued by lowering its input radiance. That points at the transfer curve rather than at the emitter, but nothing has proved which curve, and the peak-cut result must not be re-tested.

findings.problem: The sakura canopy — the largest colour accent in `hero`, occupying roughly x300-900 y100-450 — resolves at native resolution into a mass of large flat petal cards with hard aliased edges and no branch structure inside the crown. A native crop of x380-1000 y90-490 shows individual leaf polygons 40-60 px across, all at one scale, with jagged unfiltered silhouettes and visible notches where cards clip each other; no twigs, no branchlets and no small blossom clusters enter the crown, so the canopy floats as a cloud above a trunk. The shading itself is now healthy and I want to record that explicitly, because round 16's fix landed: a hue histogram over x304-870 y117-420 (170,214 chromatic pixels) is a single continuous mode at 0-10 degrees with a smooth tail to 330 and 30 degrees — 27.6% at 10, 15.7% at 0, 15.6% at 350, 11.5% at 20, 10.3% at 340 — with no separate violet population, and the canopy luma p10/p50/p90 is 79/119/162. The two-hue split is gone. What remains is silhouette and scale, not tint.
findings.why: This is the object the hero framing is composed around and it is close enough to the camera to be read as individual blossoms. At this screen size a shipped title shows blossom clusters, visible branch armature through the canopy and a soft broken edge; a mass of same-sized hard-edged cards reads as a particle sprite, and it is the first thing a stranger's eye lands on in the frame.
findings.fix: Break the canopy's single scale and soften its edge. Target: the connected-component size distribution of blossom-hued pixels inside x300-900 y100-450 must span at least a 4:1 range of areas rather than clustering at one size, and the mean-absolute-Laplacian along the crown's outer silhouette must fall by at least 30% from its current value (measure it now, before touching anything, and quote both numbers). Visible branch geometry must enter the crown from the trunk — verify by cropping x380-1000 y90-490 at native and confirming branch pixels are present inside the canopy mass, not only below it. Do NOT re-touch the leaf tint or the vertex normals: the hue histogram above shows both are correct now. Round 16 proved this crown is Props.sacredTree and not Foliage.js — a fix applied to Foliage's leaf material cannot draw a pixel of it, and that misroute already cost two rounds.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN: one card archetype instanced at one scale would produce exactly this size distribution, which would make the fix authoring variety rather than mesh density. Measure the component-size histogram first; if it is already broad, the defect is edge filtering alone and a density increase will not help.

findings.problem: The treeline in `valley` is a flat-topped wall of near-identical repeated cards running the full 2532 px of the frame, at full local contrast against a golden sky with no atmospheric lift. A native crop of x200-1400 y150-470 shows a continuous band of the same conifer silhouette repeated at the same height and the same spacing, with a stippled hard-edged foliage texture and a top edge that varies by only a small fraction of the band's own height; there is no emergent tree, no gap, no ridge behind it, and no size falloff to suggest depth within the band. Measured: box (220,120,300x50) on sky just above the band reads luma 167.04, saturation 0.552; box (220,200,300x200) on the band itself reads luma 76.02, saturation 0.417 — a 91-luma step across the horizon line, so the band takes essentially no haze lift toward the sky it sits against. For comparison the same frame's near ground at x300-800 y760-900 reads luma 58.53 at saturation 0.598, i.e. the distant forest is only 0.18 less saturated than ground three metres from the camera.
findings.why: E05-WORLD's second principle is that distance reads atmospherically or the vista is a backdrop, and its landmark principle asks for a deliberate silhouette hierarchy. A repeating hard-edged wall at the horizon does the opposite of both: it caps the frame with a fence instead of opening it, and it tells the eye the world ends there. In a blind pick this is the second thing after the flat mountain that makes ours read as a level and the reference read as a landscape.
findings.fix: Two targets on the same boxes. (a) Silhouette: the top edge of the band across x200-2300 must gain variation — measure the per-column height of the sky/canopy boundary and take its standard deviation to at least 12% of the band's mean height, with at least four emergent crowns rising more than 25% above the local mean. (b) Aerial lift: box (220,200,300x200) must close at least a third of the 91-luma gap to the sky box (220,120,300x50) at 167.04, i.e. reach luma 105 or higher, and drop saturation to 0.30 or below, while the near-ground control box (300,760,500x140) stays within 4 luma of its current 58.53 so the change is proven to be distance-dependent. Note that round 8 disproved fixing `valley` saturation from Terrain.js — the illuminant fit there forces sRGB saturation 0.593-0.609 on a perfectly achromatic ground albedo, so this must move on the foliage/aerial side, not the ground albedo side.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN: the band's uniform height and spacing look like a single scatter rule with no size or elevation jitter rather than a LOD or impostor problem. Check the placement distribution before assuming the impostor material is at fault — round 16 already found and fixed dead uniforms on that material, so a second impostor hunt is the likely wasted round here.

findings.problem: The shrine complex in `wide` has no landmark hierarchy: the honden roof, the two vermilion torii, the two pavilions and the bridge all read at roughly the same apparent height and the same tonal value, scattered across the middle band of the frame with no dominant silhouette among them. Squinting at shots/sheet-phone-r17.png, the only thing that reads as dominant in that tile is the mountain range, which is terrain rather than an authored landmark; the sakura crown is the second read, and the honden — the subject of the entire level — is a small dark roof indistinguishable in size from the pavilion beside it. Ground block means across the plaza band (12 columns x 4 rows, x60-2460, y640-1080) confirm the frame's only structure is a lantern-lit corridor at columns 5-7 (66, 60, 71 at y880-1000 against 36, 39, 41 either side); everything else is one value.
findings.why: E05-WORLD names deliberate landmark hierarchy as a principle — one dominant silhouette, a small number of secondary ones, everything else subordinate — and BM-WORLD-03 asks whether a stranger can name the dominant landmark at thumbnail scale. Here they would name the mountain, which the level did not author. Without an entry point the eye has nowhere to land and the establishing shot of the game reads as a scatter of props rather than as a place with a centre.
findings.fix: Give `wide` one authored dominant silhouette. Verifiable target: in the `wide` framing, the tallest man-made element must subtend at least 1.6x the apparent screen height of the next-tallest man-made element, and its silhouette must break the horizon line rather than sitting entirely below it. Measure both heights in pixels from the r18 `wide` capture and quote them. Second target: the honden must be separable from its neighbours by value as well as size — its roof must differ from the adjacent pavilion roof by at least 15 luma. Do not solve this by moving the camera; BM-WORLD-03 is about the layout, and Cinematic.js is not the owner.
findings.hypothesis: UNPROVEN: the plateau is flat at a single height (WORLD.PLATEAU_HEIGHT 812) and every structure stands on it, which would make equal apparent height the arithmetic consequence of the layout rather than of the individual prop scales. If that is the case, the fix is elevation or scale differentiation in the layout, not taller props. Confirm the stand heights before choosing.
